chunks.text: Summary: This workgroup report examines the necessity of mandating stock epinephrine in all U.S. schools to ensure prompt treatment of anaphylaxis. It identifies ten barriers to adoption, including liability concerns and lack of training, and proposes strategies such as legal immunity, cost stabilization advocacy, and education. The report emphasizes that voluntary stock epinephrine laws may compromise student safety and advocates for mandated legislation supported by school nurse training and partnerships.

chunks.text:
Conditions:
  - Condition id: cond_01
    Name: Anaphylaxis
    Epidemiology: Up to 29% of reported anaphylaxis cases in children occur in schools or child care centers.
chunks.chunk_id: GUIDELINE - Russell et al. - 2023 - The Need for Required Stock Epinephrine in All Schools A Work Group Report_chunk_0006
chunks.doc_id: GUIDELINE - Russell et al. - 2023 - The Need for Required Stock Epinephrine in All Schools A Work Group Report

chunks.text:
Treatment pathways:
  - Pathway id: path_01
    Condition ref: cond_01
    Setting: first_line
    Patient population: Students and staff experiencing suspected anaphylaxis in the school setting, including those with known allergies and those without prior diagnosis
    Decision rules:
    - If signs and symptoms of anaphylaxis are present, administer epinephrine immediately and activate emergency medical services.
    - Use stock epinephrine if the individual does not have their own prescribed autoinjector or it is not available.
    Recommended regimens:
    - Name: Epinephrine autoinjector (e.g., EpiPen, Auvi-Q)
    Summary: Intramuscular injection of epinephrine into the anterolateral thigh is the first-line treatment for anaphylaxis, to be administered promptly upon recognition.
    Key outcomes: Prompt epinephrine administration is associated with lower rates of mortality and near-fatality.
    Duration cycles: Single dose; may repeat every 5-15 minutes if symptoms persist
    Not recommended:
    - Name: Delayed epinephrine administration or use of antihistamines as initial treatment
    Reason: Delays in epinephrine administration are linked to poorer outcomes; antihistamines do not effectively treat cardiovascular and respiratory symptoms of anaphylaxis.
    Response assessment:
    - Timepoint: After epinephrine administration
    Method: Monitor for improvement in respiratory distress, hypotension, and skin manifestations; continue emergency care until EMS arrival.
    Supportive care:
    - Position patient supine or in a position comfortable for breathing
    - Administer oxygen if available
    - Initiate CPR if indicated
    Special considerations: Stock epinephrine must be stored in unlocked, easily accessible locations; school personnel should receive training in anaphylaxis recognition and autoinjector use; legal immunity from liability for prescribers and staff is crucial for program implementation.

chunks.text:
Recommendations:
  - Rec id: rec_01
    Statement: Allergists, allergy nurses, and other health care professionals should collaborate with national and state medical and nursing organizations, public health departments, hospital administrators, local health care professionals, and patient advocacy groups to promote mandated stock epinephrine and evidence-based anaphylaxis management programs in all K-12 schools through support, education, and advocacy at local, state, and national levels.
    Context: Addressed to allergists, allergy nurses, and other health care professionals.
    Source heading: CONCLUSIONS / Workgroup Recommendations (Table V)
  - Rec id: rec_02
    Statement: They should educate primary care physicians about school stock epinephrine barriers and jointly collaborate and advocate at district, local, state, and national levels.
    Context: Addressed to allergists, allergy nurses, and other health care professionals.
    Source heading: CONCLUSIONS / Workgroup Recommendations (Table V)
  - Rec id: rec_03
    Statement: They should partner with medical and nursing organizations, hospital administrators, and patient advocacy groups to advocate to school boards and administrators for state mandates that include dedicated funding to hire more full-time school nurses, aiming for at least one school nurse per school.
    Context: Addressed to allergists, allergy nurses, and other health care professionals.
    Source heading: CONCLUSIONS / Workgroup Recommendations (Table V)
  - Rec id: rec_04
    Statement: They should offer authoritative recommendations and advocacy to advance laws, regulations, and district policies in every state that permit school nurses to train and supervise unlicensed assistive personnel in medication administration.
    Context: Addressed to allergists, allergy nurses, and other health care professionals.
    Source heading: CONCLUSIONS / Workgroup Recommendations (Table V)
  - Rec id: rec_05
    Statement: National and state medical and nursing organizations should pass resolutions and position statements endorsing a legal requirement for stock epinephrine in all K-12 schools nationwide.
    Context: Addressed to national and state medical and nursing organizations.
    Source heading: CONCLUSIONS / Workgroup Recommendations (Table V)
  - Rec id: rec_06
    Statement: They should advocate to school boards and administrators for state mandates that provide targeted funding to employ more full-time school nurses, with the goal of one school nurse in each school.
    Context: Addressed to national and state medical and nursing organizations.
    Source heading: CONCLUSIONS / Workgroup Recommendations (Table V)
  - Rec id: rec_07
    Statement: They should provide authoritative recommendations and advocacy to support laws, regulations, and district policies in all states that enable school nurses to train and oversee unlicensed assistive personnel for medication administration.
    Context: Addressed to national and state medical and nursing organizations.
    Source heading: CONCLUSIONS / Workgroup Recommendations (Table V)
  - Rec id: rec_08
    Statement: They should advocate for amendments to existing state legislation to establish requirements for sustainable school-based anaphylaxis management programs, including standards for training content and trainer qualifications.
    Context: Addressed to national and state medical and nursing organizations.
    Source heading: CONCLUSIONS / Workgroup Recommendations (Table V)
  - Rec id: rec_09
    Statement: Epinephrine auto-injector manufacturers should provide a single-dose packaging option instead of only dual-dose packs.
    Context: Addressed to epinephrine delivery device manufacturers.
    Source heading: CONCLUSIONS / Workgroup Recommendations (Table V)
  - Rec id: rec_10
    Statement: Manufacturers should offer discounted pricing for epinephrine auto-injectors to schools.
    Context: Addressed to epinephrine delivery device manufacturers.
    Source heading: CONCLUSIONS / Workgroup Recommendations (Table V)
  - Rec id: rec_11
    Statement: Every state should enact legislation requiring stock epinephrine in all K-12 schools and include a Good Samaritan indemnification clause.
    Context: Addressed to states.
    Source heading: CONCLUSIONS / Workgroup Recommendations (Table V)
  - Rec id: rec_12
    Statement: States should draft, pass, or modify stock epinephrine legislation to incorporate sustainable, targeted funding for school districts to hire additional school nurses and cover the extra time and workload associated with school anaphylaxis management programs.
    Context: Addressed to states.
    Source heading: CONCLUSIONS / Workgroup Recommendations (Table V)
  - Rec id: rec_13
    Statement: States should mandate standardized reporting of stock epinephrine and epinephrine auto-injector administrations, along with related data, from all schools using the NASN's Report Form for Epinephrine Administration, with collected data made accessible to researchers.
    Context: Addressed to states.
    Source heading: CONCLUSIONS / Workgroup Recommendations (Table V)
  - Rec id: rec_14
    Statement: States should establish comprehensive statewide systems for reporting, collecting, and analyzing data related to school anaphylaxis management, health outcomes, and usage of epinephrine auto-injectors and stock epinephrine.
    Context: Addressed to states.
    Source heading: CONCLUSIONS / Workgroup Recommendations (Table V)

chunks.text:
Artifacts:
  Artifact id: art_01
  Type: figure
  Title: Strengthening the safety chain to support school SE
  Source heading: INTRODUCTION
  Description: A concept map centered on 'School Stock Epinephrine'. Surrounding it are four primary barrier categories: UNDIAGNOSED STUDENTS & STAFF (first allergic reaction, no prescribed EDD), DIAGNOSED STUDENTS & STAFF (lacks prescribed EDD), FINANCE (EDD cost and access barriers), and LAWS (state legal mandate vs. voluntary coverage). An outer ring shows areas requiring education and advocacy: SCHOOL (board and administrator resistance), SCHOOL NURSES (presence and caseload disparities), CLINICAL TEAM (prescriber concerns, school forms challenges), and SCHOOL STAFF (absent or inconsistent anaphylaxis training, liability concerns). Arrows indicate that education and advocacy strengthen the chain supporting SE.
  Summary: A concept map summarizing barriers to stock epinephrine in schools and the dual role of education and advocacy to mitigate them.
  Clinical relevance: Helps identify leverage points for interventions to improve epinephrine access and anaphylaxis safety in schools.

  Title: Potential barriers to safe school medication administration
  Source heading: Barrier 5: Difficulties regarding delegation of medication administration to unlicensed assistive personnel
  Data:

      Barrier: Inconsistent medication administration delegation laws, regulations, and policies among and within states.
    Row 2:
      Barrier: Inadequate quantity of RNs staffing and directing school health programs.
    Row 3:
      Barrier: Lack of trained personnel, related policies, and procedures.

  Clinical relevance: Highlights systemic issues that compromise medication safety for students, especially those requiring emergency epinephrine.

      Objective: Identify common causes of allergic reactions.
    Row 2:
      Objective: Identify the signs and symptoms of a mild and severe allergic reaction (anaphylaxis).
    Row 3:
      Objective: Identify how signs and symptoms of anaphylaxis differ from those of other medical conditions.
    Row 4:
      Objective: Demonstrate knowing when epinephrine should be administered and when it should not be administered.
    Row 5:
      Objective: Demonstrate determining the correct dose of autoinjector, adult or pediatric, to administer.
    Row 6:
      Objective: Demonstrate the steps for administering epinephrine by an autoinjector.
    Row 7:
      Objective: Describe the methods for safely storing and handling epinephrine and appropriately disposing of the autoinjector after use.
    Row 8:
      Objective: Demonstrate the steps for providing for ongoing care of the patient until Emergency Medical Services arrives.
    Row 9:
      Objective: Demonstrate knowledge of appropriate documentation and reporting of an event in which an epinephrine autoinjector was administered.
    Row 10:
      Objective: Understand the New York state laws that allow an individual to possess and use an epinephrine autoinjector in a life-threatening situation.
  Summary: New York state requirements for school stock epinephrine training programs, covering anaphylaxis recognition, epinephrine administration, post-care, documentation, and legal aspects.
  Clinical relevance: Provides a model for evidence-based anaphylaxis training content to ensure staff competency in emergency response.

chunks.text:
Artifacts:
  Artifact id: art_04
  Type: table
  Title: NASN-recommended key components of a comprehensive anaphylaxis management school policy
  Source heading: Barrier 8: Obstacles associated with school administrators and school boards
  Data:
    Row 1:
      Component: 1. Individuals covered
      Description: Including those with first-time anaphylaxis emergencies.
    Row 2:
      Component: 2. School programs and environments covered
    Row 3:
      Component: 3. Epinephrine
      Description: School prescription and standing order. Stock locations, usually multiple—with signage. Ensured secured access. Stock supply: dosages; number of doses. Procurement: initial and periodic. Disposal: after use and expiration. Administration and documentation. Reporting.
    Row 4:
      Component: 4. Individuals authorized to administer
    Row 5:
      Component: 5. Emergency protocol for administration
    Row 6:
      Component: 6. Education, training, notification
      Description: When to administer. Who will be educated: every staff member needs to be trained to know signs and symptoms of anaphylaxis and know how to initiate the emergency protocol. Levels of education to be provided. Parent notification.
    Row 7:
      Component: 7. Communication plan
      Description: For the district, school, parents, health care provider, Emergency Medical Services, and community (part of a school’s all-hazard emergency plan).
  Summary: Seven components recommended by NASN for a comprehensive school anaphylaxis policy, including coverage, epinephrine management, authorization, training, and communication.
  Clinical relevance: Guides schools in developing robust anaphylaxis policies that ensure timely access to epinephrine and staff preparedness.

Artifacts:
  Artifact id: art_05
  Type: table
  Title: Summarized barriers to school SE and potential improvement strategies
  Source heading: CONCLUSIONS
  Data:
    Row 1:
      Barriers to school se: Indemnification concerns of prescribers and school staff
      Improvement strategies: Ensure legal immunity from liability in every state.
    Row 2:
      Barriers to school se: EDD cost
      Improvement strategies: Use free or low-cost school EDD programs from EDD manufacturer and advocate for more similar programs from additional pharmaceutical companies. Advocate for targeted state funding to school districts.
    Row 3:
      Barriers to school se: EDD access factors
      Improvement strategies: Advocate for legislation to increase EDD supply at stabilized cost. Expand EDD generic options. Increase awareness of physicians and nurses regarding all EDD options. Work to address EDD shortages. Advocate for 1 EDD injector pack option.
    Row 4:
      Barriers to school se: Lack of SNs or inadequate quantity of SNs per student and school needs
      Improvement strategies: Increase number of SNs in school districts with aim of at least 1 per school. Clarify accurate SN educational preparedness, scope of practice, and role. Promote understanding of benefits of full-time SNs in every school. Use SN staffing models on the basis of individual school and student indicators. Increase recruitment, retainment, and available funding for full-time SNs.
    Row 5:
      Barriers to school se: Absence of or inconsistent quality of comprehensive evidence-based anaphylaxis training of school UAP
      Improvement strategies: Increase awareness of available free or low-cost peer-reviewed training materials. Promote understanding of SN competency as leaders in providing comprehensive anaphylaxis management education to UAP.
    Row 6:
      Barriers to school se: Obstacles to delegating medication administration to school UAP by SNs
      Improvement strategies: Promote legal ability for SNs to delegate medication administration to school UAP. Advocate for at least 1 full-time SN in every school building. Ensure incentives to increase quantity of willing school UAP to be SN trained and supervised for medication administration.
    Row 7:
      Barriers to school se: Licensed prescriber hesitancy or absence of sufficient quantity of willing licensed prescribers for school SE
      Improvement strategies: Improve quantity of willing licensed prescribers by using school or district physicians when present and/or local physicians, including those from local health departments. Advocate for state legislation as needed to require state department of health designate a default prescribing physician if no willing local physicians are available. Provide accurate information on immunity from liability per state laws and regulations. Ensure availability of toolkits containing current resources and materials to facilitate licensed prescriber ease in ordering school SE.
    Row 8:
      Barriers to school se: Legislative challenges
      Improvement strategies: Improve legislative support for mandated school SE in all states.
    Row 9:
      Barriers to school se: School administration and school board factors
      Improvement strategies: Provide advocacy and education to schools on merits of SE. Promote support of SNs. Counsel that ample time is needed for provision of effective anaphylaxis education to school personnel.
    Row 10:
      Barriers to school se: Health care provider factors
      Improvement strategies: Use collaborative team approach to school anaphylaxis management with family/student, SN, school staff, and student’s clinical physicians and nurses. Provision by clinical teams of current and complete student-specific anaphylaxis action plans and school medication forms to patients/families and schools at start of academic year and as needed. Educate schools on the need for SE for students with no prior diagnosis of anaphylaxis.
    Row 11:
      Barriers to school se: Family and student factors
      Improvement strategies: Provision of comprehensive culturally competent anaphylaxis education to students/families by SNs and student’s clinical team of physicians and nurses. Delivery of all necessary completed medical and medication forms to schools by family/student.
  Summary: Comprehensive table pairing ten barriers to school stock epinephrine with corresponding improvement strategies, covering indemnification, cost, access, staffing, training, delegation, prescriber issues, legislation, administration, and family factors.
  Clinical relevance: Serves as a roadmap for stakeholders to address the multifaceted obstacles to making epinephrine available in schools.

chunks.text:
Artifacts:
  Artifact id: art_06
  Type: table
  Title: Workgroup recommendations
  Source heading: CONCLUSIONS
  Data:
    Row 1:
      Stakeholder: Allergists, allergy nurses, and other health care professionals
      Recommendation: Partner with national and state medical and nursing organizations; public health departments; hospital administrators; local health care professionals; and patient advocacy organizations to support, educate, and advocate at the local, state, and national level for mandated school SE and evidence-based anaphylaxis management programs in all K-12 schools. Educate primary care colleagues on school SE barriers and mutually collaborate and advocate on these issues together on a district, local, state, and national level. Partner with medical and nursing organizations, hospital administrators, and patient advocacy organizations to provide advocacy to school boards and administrators for state mandates that include targeted funding to hire more full-time SNs with the aim of at least 1 SN in every school. Provide authoritative recommendations and advocacy efforts to promote laws, regulations, and district policies in every state addressing need to allow SNs to train and supervise UAPs for medication administration.
    Row 2:
      Stakeholder: National and state medical and nursing organizations
      Recommendation: Pass resolutions and/or position statements supporting a legal mandate for SE in every K-12 school in all states. Provide advocacy to school boards and school administrators for state mandates that include targeted funding to hire more full-time SNs with the aim of 1 SN in every school. Provide authoritative recommendations and advocacy efforts promoting laws, regulations, and district policies in every state addressing need to allow SNs to train and supervise UAPs for medication administration. Advocate for amendments of current state legislation to address requirements for sustainable school-based anaphylaxis management programs, training content standards, and required trainer qualifications.
    Row 3:
      Stakeholder: Epinephrine Delivery Device Manufacturers
      Recommendation: Offer consumers a packaged 1-dose single EDD as an option vs only dual-dose packs. Provide schools with discounted pricing for EDDs.
    Row 4:
      Stakeholder: States
      Recommendation: All states should have legislation mandating SE in all K-12 schools that also includes a Good Samaritan clause for indemnification. Craft, pass, and/or amend state SE legislation to include sustainable targeted funding for districts to hire more SNs and to cover their additional time and workload related to school anaphylaxis management programming. Require standardized reporting of SE and EDD administration and related factors from all schools by using NASN’s Report Form for Epinephrine Administration with subsequent data collected by the state with researcher accessibility. Develop comprehensive state-wide data reporting, collection, and analysis of factors related to school anaphylaxis management, health outcomes, and use of EDD and SE.
  Summary: Actionable recommendations for four stakeholder groups (healthcare professionals, medical/nursing organizations, EDD manufacturers, states) to advance mandated school stock epinephrine and comprehensive anaphylaxis management.
  Clinical relevance: Provides a framework for coordinated advocacy and policy change to enhance school safety for children at risk of anaphylaxis.

Artifacts:
  Artifact id: art_07
  Type: table
  Title: Future research recommendations
  Source heading: CONCLUSIONS
  Data:
    Row 1:
      Research recommendation: Study collected data regarding school anaphylaxis management and epinephrine administration between states with SE mandates vs states that voluntarily allow SE.
    Row 2:
      Research recommendation: Compare student health outcomes from anaphylaxis between schools in states with mandated SE vs those in states that legally allow SE on a voluntary basis.
    Row 3:
      Research recommendation: Explore school reporting and state data collection of school EDD and SE administration and whether these data are publicly available.
    Row 4:
      Research recommendation: Investigate implementation of standardized school reporting of EDD and SE administration and related factors through use of NASN’s Report Form for Epinephrine Administration with subsequent data collected by state.
    Row 5:
      Research recommendation: Study the role of indemnification in school decision making regarding SE and provision of SN-led anaphylaxis management staff training.
    Row 6:
      Research recommendation: Study evaluation data on effectiveness and health outcomes associated with elements of school-based anaphylaxis management training.
    Row 7:
      Research recommendation: Ongoing investigation of school SE benefits related to reduction in health care disparities, cost to families, other social determinants of health issues, and environmental impact, while increasing ability to treat unanticipated anaphylaxis in students with no known history of allergy and those lacking prescribed EDDs.
  Summary: Seven research priorities to evaluate the impact of mandated versus voluntary stock epinephrine, effectiveness of training, reporting systems, and health equity.
  Clinical relevance: Identifies evidence gaps to inform future policies and best practices for school anaphylaxis management.

  Title: Public education governance structure, simplified
  Source heading: Barrier 8: Obstacles associated with school administrators and school boards
  Description: A hierarchical diagram showing layers of public education governance from top to bottom: Federal, State, District (School Board), and School (Administrators).
